22420-the-book-of-nature-myths:
The Book of Nature Myths retells tales that explain the natural world. Its opening story begins long ago, when the earth was very young. Two hunters travel through a forest far from home.

They have tracked a deer for many days by then. Night falls, dark and gloomy, around the hunters. Then a bright light comes in the western sky. Such a moment launches a myth of sky or star. The collection gathers such explanatory stories for young readers. Each tale answers a child's question about nature with a story. It preserves folk imagination in simple, clear retellings meant to be read aloud.
22518-quaint-epitaphs:
Quaint Epitaphs gathers curious inscriptions from gravestones into one book. Its compiler trusted readers would not call the book presumptuous. Many epitaph collections already existed when she published hers.

Requests for a look at her private collection prompted publication. Friends asked to examine it so often that printing followed. Graveyard verses preserve humor, grief, and local character in stone. A good epitaph can sum up a life in four lines. The compiler's haul comes from churchyards near and far. Readers get to wander cemeteries without leaving their chairs. The book charms by turns: funny, pious, odd, and sometimes deeply touching in brevity.
22693-a-book-of-myths:
A Book of Myths retells the great stories of Greek and other ancient myth for general readers. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Retellings of this era aimed to give children and busy adults the tales of gods and heroes in clear, handsome prose, with the worst crudities softened.

The sample's opening passage wrestles honestly with the gods' bad behavior. It wonders how heroes who fell fighting by the Scamander came to be worshipped as more than men. Such reflections frame the stories of Troy and Olympus that follow. The book belongs to the shelf of myth handbooks that formed the classical imagination of English-speaking readers. It still offers a graceful first path into the old tales.
23164-the-creature-from-cleveland-depths:
Fritz Leiber kicks a television in The Creature from Cleveland Depths. Gusterson gives the dead television a sour kick on his way past. If the company had use for them, he grumbles, it would pay them something. Wrong, his friend answers. Money never was the right goad for inner-directed men like Gussy, straight from the Motivations chief's own mouth.

Leiber sets his satire in a burrowed future Cleveland, where underground life runs on motivational jargon and gadgets that manage their owners. The creature of the title grows out of that managed world, part pet, part product, all consequence. Fay and Gussy argue their way through it in Leiber's wittiest register. The story predicts wearable masters with unnerving cheer, and remains very funny about a future that arrived on schedule.
c-f-meyer-die-hochzeit-des-monchs:
A monk leaves his monastery for love, and the consequences unfold like a dark fairy tale in C. F. Meyer's Die Hochzeit des Moenchs, given here in German. The Monk's Wedding is framed as a story told at Dante's tomb in Verona, which lends the telling a solemn music. Passion stands against vows throughout the novella.

The frame's listeners interrupt, question, and darken the tale as it proceeds, a device Meyer handles beautifully. Medieval atmosphere thickens around a very modern psychology of desire and guilt. The monk's choice echoes outward until no one in the story stands untouched. Haunting is the word readers reach for with this one. It shows the master's late manner at full strength.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cloths: A 1913 entry on altar cloths — the three linen covers of the mensa. Augustin Schulte sets out the rubrics. Their whiteness clothes the sacrifice. The topmost bears the cross's mark. Linen for the Lord's table. Their hems are edged with lace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andechs: This 1913 reference piece on Andechs — the Holy Mountain of Bavaria. Michael Ott tells its pilgrim story. Its relics draw a million feet. Beer and prayer meet on its hill. Bavaria's beloved shrine. Its monks brew the famous beer. Its festival draws the Munich crowds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casimir-ubagh: This 1913 reference piece on Casimir Ubaghs — a Louvain philosopher of note. Maurice De Wulf records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the Belgian schools. A teacher of the nineteenth century. His Theodicea served the Louvain schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-post-: This 1913 reference article on English post-Reformation oaths — the penal tests. John Hungerford Pollen unfolds their cruel forms. The supremacy oath trapped the faithful. The recusants paid the heavy fines. The snares of the persecuting law. Their 1606 allegiance is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu: This 1913 reference article on Fuchs — the Austrian chemist. Thomas O'Conor Sloane honors his mineral labors. His science probed the stony earth. The Academy prized its learned son. The cabinets keep his name. His 1856 death is famed. His 1856 minerals are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oaths: An oath calls God to witness the truth, and this entry examines its morality, its kinds, and its abuses. A careful moral treatment of swearing. The sacred weight of a promise: the entry weighs oaths, vows, and perjury with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostrogoths: The Ostrogoths were the eastern Goths who ruled Italy under Theodoric the Great. This entry traces their kingdom, their Arian faith, and their fall to Justinian. The barbarians who became Romans: their kingdom preserved much of the classical past intact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-special-devot: Special devotions for months assign each month a mystery. This entry surveys their calendar, their prayers, and their history. The piety of the monthly cycle: their twelve months fill the year in the calendar of the Church in the missal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-griffi: Griffiths was the vicar of London. This entry traces his 1800s, his district, and his labors. The bishop of the London faithful: his vast district crowned London in the 1830s of the Poynter in the truly very old brick chapel.
govdocs-archive_org-KlausFuchs_Klaus_Fuc: An FBI records-review inventory sheet for the New York files logs the bureau's holdings on Klaus Fuchs. Fuchs was the physicist who spied for the Soviet Union from inside the atomic bomb project. Review sheets record what a file holds and where its parts were sent, here between the Bureau and Albuquerque among others. He confessed in 1950. The sheet is pure paperwork: declassified inventory from the handling of the Cold War's most damaging espionage case.
our-friend-john-burroughs: Clara Barrus, Burroughs's friend and biographer, paints an intimate portrait of the great American nature writer at his Catskills home, Slabsides. She recalls his conversations, his walks, his humor, and the stream of famous visitors — from Roosevelt to Edison. A warm, personal memoir of a man who taught America to love its birds and woods.
self-raised-or-from-the-depths: E. D. E. N. Southworth was the bestselling American novelist of her century, and this melodrama shows her powers at full stretch. Her hero climbs from the depths of misfortune through pluck, virtue, and no small number of startling twists. Victorian readers devoured such stories by the million; modern readers will find a lively window into what the 1800s loved to read.
the-doom-of-the-griffiths: Elizabeth Gaskell's Welsh story about the doom of the Griffiths: a family's curse in the mountains. Dark and romantic, it shows her Celtic imagination. A powerful early tale. The Welsh mountains brood over this dark tale.
the-two-paths: John Ruskin's Two Paths contrasts the way of art and the way of industry — lectures on beauty's place in modern life. His eloquent plea for the lovely shaped a generation. Art criticism as moral prophecy. His gospel of beauty challenged the iron age of machinery.
